intro: AI tools for journalists and reporters on Mac help with the work around the story. For most reporters that means email, research, dictation and a last pass on copy. Lazur is a voice assistant that sees your screen, points at things, answers out loud and drafts text you can paste. It does not write your story or send your email for you.

blocks.text: A reporter's day rarely follows the plan. You chase a source, wait on a clerk, read a long agenda and rewrite the same paragraph more than once. The editor wants the story by five. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics describes the core work as researching assigned topics, interviewing people and writing stories for newspapers, magazines or websites.
Where a reporter's time really goes

The public numbers on this are thin. The searches turned up no recent survey that splits a reporter's day into email, admin, research and writing. The BLS page describes the duties but gives no time shares. It says reporters spend some time in an office, often travel to cover events, and can file stories remotely. That mix means no two days look the same.

Read these numbers as signals, not measurements. Microsoft's figures come from an early 2023 study of workers in general, not journalists. The 4.3 hours comes from Fyxer, which publishes it on its own blog, so treat it with care. Still, the direction is clear enough to plan around. Email and messages take a big share of office time, and a reporter's inbox is part of that office time.
Why email and admin take the hours

Email grows around a story. A press office sends a statement. A source copies three people. A clerk replies with an attachment and a new deadline. Each message needs a reply, a filing note or a forward. Microsoft's 2023 study put the heaviest users, the top quarter of email users, at 8.8 hours a week over a rolling 28-day period ending March 2023.
Admin also hides in small tasks. Each one takes a minute, and together they fill the gaps between calls. These are the ones that pile up on most reporters' Macs.

items: Replies to press offices and clerks, with the same few answers every week.
Interview notes typed up from memory or from a voice memo.
Figures from budgets, votes or public records that need one clean table.
Calendar changes after a source moves a call to another day.
Copy that needs a trim, a headline check and a name check before the desk sees it.

blocks.text: Which AI tools for journalists and reporters handle each task

Lazur does not sit in your inbox or write your story. It works on your screen, one request at a time, through a fixed set of ways to help. Explain answers questions about what is on screen. Point circles where something is. Guide walks you through a menu, one click at a time, and waits for each click. Dictate types clean text at your cursor. Draft writes text you can paste. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and comes back with a summary and a report. Everyday covers timers, Apple Reminders, Calendar events, notes, music, opening apps and links, web search and Shortcuts.

blocks.text: Match the capability to the task. Use point when you know the thing exists but cannot find it. Use guide when you know the goal but not the menu path. Use draft only when you already know what the message should say. Lazur fills in the words, and you decide what goes out.
A realistic day with Lazur

The day below is one plausible shape for a local reporter. It is not a survey result. Notice the pattern. The reporter asks for one thing at a time, checks the answer and keeps the decisions. Short requests work better than long ones, because each one gets a clear answer you can check.
Research without losing the thread

Research is the task that eats the most time and carries the most risk. Lazur runs research jobs in its own Chrome tabs, apart from the tabs you use for work. When the job finishes, you get a summary and a report. Ask for the source of every claim. Then open each link yourself before any name or number goes into a draft.

Narrow questions get better answers. 'Tell me about the budget' is too wide. 'Find the vote counts for the last few council budget votes, with links to the minutes' gives you a list to check. Treat the report as a set of leads. A research job can return a wrong date or a name that does not match the record.
Dictation and notes on deadline

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Dictation is unlimited on both paid plans, so you can type your interview notes straight after the call. Store council members' names, street names and a source's company spelling in the personal dictionary. Snippets hold the lines you type every day, such as your contact details for a press office.

Clipboard slots help when you move a quote from a PDF into a draft. Copy the quote, then the citation, and keep both ready. Always check dictated quotes against the recording before they go into your copy. Speech tools mishear names and figures, and a wrong figure in print is hard to undo.
Google Docs, Word and Slack on a reporter's Mac

Most drafts live in Google Docs or Word. Google Docs runs in the browser. Google's accessibility help describes it as a web application and recommends the latest Chrome. For a menu step, open Tools > Word count to check a length. Lazur sees the Docs tab like any other window, so ask it where things are instead of hunting through the toolbar. See [Google Docs for journalists on Mac](/for/journalists/google-docs) for a closer look.

Word for Mac has its own ribbon and its own Review tab. For edits, open Review > Track Changes. If you cannot find that button, ask Lazur to walk you through it, and it circles the button when it appears on screen. The editing and proof steps are in [Word for journalists on Mac](/for/journalists/word).

blocks.title: Check Office before a deadline
blocks.text: Microsoft says Microsoft 365 subscribers on Mac, and people with one-time-purchase Office 2019 or 2021 on Mac, may enter reduced functionality mode from July 13, 2026. In that mode you can open and print files but not edit, save or create them. Check Microsoft's page before you rely on Word.

Newsdesk Slack channels move fast during a story. Use ⌘ K to jump to a conversation, and mute any channel you do not need during a shift. The steps are in [how to jump to a conversation in Slack](/how-to/jump-to-a-conversation-in-slack) and [how to mute a channel in Slack](/how-to/mute-a-channel-in-slack).
Sources, drafts and newsroom rules

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer you. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those are the product's stated rules. They do not replace your newsroom's rules, and this page does not claim any certification for newsroom use.

Your paper's policy on sources comes first. If it bars sending source names, phone numbers or unpublished copy to outside services, follow that rule. Ask your editor or legal desk what applies to your work before you hold the shortcut near those files. A quick check now saves a hard conversation later.

blocks.title: Close the file first
blocks.text: Before you hold the shortcut, close or hide anything that shows a confidential source, a home address or an unpublished document you have not cleared to share.
Mistakes reporters make with AI tools

items: Asking a broad question. Ask for one thing, with a name, a date or a document attached.
Trusting a summary without opening the link behind it.
Pasting a whole file when one page would do. A smaller piece of text makes the answer easier to check.
Letting a drafted line turn into a quote. Quotes come from the recording or your notes.
Skipping the newsroom rule on confidential material because the tool feels private.
Waiting for the trial to end in the middle of a story. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) before a heavy week.

blocks.text: A tool that writes fast can also write wrong. Check every name, figure and date against the source before it goes to the editor. Lazur drafts and types text. The byline, the reporting and the decision to publish stay with you.
What to do next

Download Lazur for Mac and open it once. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. The Pro trial starts when you first open the app, and it needs no credit card. [Download Lazur](/download) to start.

Pick one task from your week that you repeat, such as the clerk emails or the interview notes. Run that one task through Lazur for a few days. Keep what saves time and drop what gets in the way. One task done well beats a full setup you abandon by Friday.

faq.question: What are the best AI tools for journalists and reporters on Mac?
faq.answer: There is no single best tool, so match the tool to the task. Apple's Mail User Guide for Mac covers the built-in Mail app, which handles most email. Use the research tools your newsroom approves for sourcing. Lazur covers the voice side of the work. It points at what is on your screen, answers out loud, dictates text and drafts lines you can paste.

faq.question: Does Lazur work inside Google Docs and Word?
faq.answer: Lazur works in any app on your Mac, because it sees your screen. It is not a plugin or add-in for Google Docs or Word, and it has no partnership with either maker. It points at buttons and guides you through menus, one click at a time. It does not type into the document unless you dictate.

faq.question: Can Lazur click buttons or edit my files?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It points, explains, guides and answers out loud. It drafts text you can paste, and you decide what goes into the document.

faq.question: Is it safe to use with confidential sources?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Your newsroom's rules on sources come first. This page does not claim any certification for newsroom use, so ask your editor what applies.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

faq.question: How much does Lazur cost for a reporter?
faq.answer: The Pro trial starts when you first open the app, and it needs no credit card. Paid plans come with monthly or annual billing. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) for current prices. Dictation is unlimited on both paid plans.

faq.question: Can I publish research that Lazur returns?
faq.answer: Not without checking it first. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and comes back with a summary and a report. Open each source yourself, confirm names, dates and figures, and check every quote against your notes or the recording.

faq.question: What should a reporter try first?
faq.answer: Start with one task you repeat each week, such as clerk emails or interview notes. Use it for a few days, then decide whether it saves you time. Point and dictate are quick to check, so they make good first tries.

painPoints.title: Email fills the gaps
painPoints.text: The heaviest email users in Microsoft's 2023 study spent 8.8 hours a week on email. Press office replies and clerk emails land in the same inbox as your story notes.

painPoints.title: Admin sits between the good parts
painPoints.text: Replies, calendar changes and file names take small slices of time. They come between calls and writing, so the writing often starts late.

painPoints.title: Research with no clear finish
painPoints.text: Agendas, past coverage and background reading can run on for hours. It is hard to tell when you have read enough to write.

painPoints.title: Interview notes go stale
painPoints.text: Notes typed from memory lose detail by the afternoon. Typing up a call can take a long stretch of an already full day.

painPoints.title: A last pass before the desk
painPoints.text: A draft may need trimming, a name check and a quote check on the same deadline. Each pass is small, but they stack up by late afternoon.

painPoints.title: Travel changes the shape of the day
painPoints.text: The BLS says reporters travel to cover events and can file stories remotely. One story can mean a desk day, and the next a field day.
